questions.q: Which International Union of Biochemistry and Molecular Biology (IUBMB) enzyme class catalyzes oxidation-reduction reactions?
questions.explain: EC 1 (oxidoreductases) catalyze electron or hydrogen transfer in oxidation-reduction reactions, such as dehydrogenases and oxidases. Transferases (EC 2) move functional groups, hydrolases (EC 3) cleave bonds using water, and ligases (EC 6) join molecules using ATP.

open.q: Which main IUBMB enzyme class (EC 1) catalyzes oxidation-reduction reactions?

questions.q: Which enzyme class catalyzes the joining of two substrates coupled to the cleavage of a nucleoside triphosphate such as ATP?
questions.explain: Ligases (EC 6, synthetases) form new covalent bonds (such as C-C, C-S, C-O, or C-N) using energy from ATP or another nucleoside triphosphate. Lyases (EC 4) cleave or form bonds without hydrolysis or oxidation, often creating double bonds.

open.q: Which class of enzymes (EC 6) catalyzes bond formation coupled to ATP hydrolysis?

questions.q: Which enzyme class catalyzes intramolecular structural or geometric rearrangements within a single molecule?
questions.explain: Isomerases (EC 5) catalyze isomerization within a single substrate, including racemases, epimerases, and mutases (such as phosphoglycerate mutase). Transferases (EC 2) transfer groups between different molecules.

open.q: Which enzyme class (EC 5) catalyzes intramolecular rearrangement to form isomers?

questions.q: What is the non-protein organic molecule tightly or covalently bound to an enzyme required for its catalytic activity?
questions.explain: A prosthetic group is a tightly or covalently attached non-protein organic cofactor (such as FAD in succinate dehydrogenase or heme). An apoenzyme plus its required cofactor(s) forms a catalytically active holoenzyme.

open.q: What term describes a tightly or covalently bound non-protein organic group essential for an enzyme's function?

questions.q: What is an inactive precursor of an enzyme that requires proteolytic cleavage to become catalytically active?
questions.explain: Zymogens (proenzymes), such as pepsinogen, trypsinogen, and chymotrypsinogen, are synthesized as inactive precursors and activated by selective peptide bond cleavage. This prevents premature self-digestion of producing cells or tissues.

open.q: What term denotes an inactive enzyme precursor activated by proteolytic cleavage?

questions.q: How does an enzyme accelerate the rate of a biochemical reaction?
options: Lowers the activation energy barrier of the transition state
Makes a thermodynamically unfavorable reaction have a negative delta G
Changes the equilibrium constant (Keq) of the reaction
Is permanently consumed during each catalytic cycle
questions.explain: Enzymes stabilize the transition state and lower activation energy (delta G double-dagger), increasing both forward and reverse reaction rates equally without altering delta G or Keq. They emerge unchanged at the end of catalysis.

open.q: By what energetic mechanism do enzymes increase the rate of a chemical reaction?
accept: stabilizing the transition state and lowering activation energy

questions.q: According to transition-state theory, why does an enzyme bind the transition state much more tightly than the ground-state substrate?
options: Tighter transition-state binding lowers the free energy barrier between substrate and transition state
Tighter ground-state binding deep in an energy well speeds up catalysis
Transition-state binding reverses the equilibrium constant of the reaction
Transition-state binding prevents product release from the active site
questions.explain: Preferential binding and stabilization of the transition state relative to the ground-state substrate lowers the activation energy required to reach the transition state. Excessively tight binding to the ground state would deepen the energy well and slow reaction rate.

open.q: Why must an enzyme's active site be complementary to the transition state rather than the ground-state substrate?
accept: stabilizing the transition state lowers the activation energy barrier

questions.q: Which model of enzyme-substrate interaction proposes that the enzyme's active site undergoes a conformational change upon substrate binding?
questions.explain: The induced-fit model (Koshland) states that substrate binding induces a conformational change in the enzyme to align catalytic groups precisely. The rigid lock-and-key model assumes a pre-shaped active site matching the substrate.

open.q: Which model describes conformational adjustment of an enzyme's active site upon binding substrate?

questions.q: In Michaelis-Menten kinetics, what does the Michaelis constant (Km) represent?
options: The substrate concentration at which reaction velocity is half of Vmax
The maximum reaction velocity at saturating substrate concentration
The turnover number of a single enzyme active site per second
The inhibitor concentration that reduces Vmax by half
questions.explain: Km is defined as the substrate concentration [S] required to achieve 0.5 Vmax. Under standard assumptions (k-1 + k2 >> k1), a lower Km indicates higher apparent affinity of the enzyme for its substrate.

open.q: How is the Michaelis constant (Km) defined in enzyme kinetics?

questions.q: What does the turnover number (kcat) of an enzyme measure?
options: Substrate molecules converted per active site per unit time at saturation
Free-energy change between reactants and products
questions.explain: Turnover number (kcat = Vmax / [E]total) expresses how many catalytic cycles one enzyme molecule or active site completes per second under saturating substrate. Catalytic efficiency is often assessed by the kcat/Km ratio.

open.q: What quantity does the turnover number (kcat) of an enzyme represent?
accept: catalytic events per active site per second
substrate molecules converted per enzyme per second at saturation
number of turnovers per unit time per enzyme site

questions.q: On a Lineweaver-Burk (double-reciprocal) plot of 1/V versus 1/[S], what does the y-intercept equal?
questions.explain: Rearranging the Michaelis-Menten equation gives 1/V = (Km/Vmax)(1/[S]) + 1/Vmax, which is linear with slope Km/Vmax and y-intercept 1/Vmax. Extrapolating the line to 1/V = 0 gives an x-intercept of -1/Km.

open.q: What value corresponds to the y-intercept on a Lineweaver-Burk double-reciprocal plot?

questions.q: What is the characteristic kinetic effect of a pure competitive inhibitor on an enzyme-catalyzed reaction?
options: Increases apparent Km while leaving Vmax unchanged
Decreases Vmax while leaving Km unchanged
Decreases both Km and Vmax equally
questions.explain: A competitive inhibitor binds reversibly to the free enzyme active site, competing with substrate and increasing apparent Km (requiring higher [S] for half-maximal rate). Because high [S] outcompetes the inhibitor, Vmax can still be reached.

open.q: How does a competitive inhibitor alter apparent Km and Vmax of an enzyme?
accept: increases apparent Km and leaves Vmax unchanged
raises Km with no change in Vmax

questions.q: Which type of reversible inhibitor binds exclusively to the enzyme-substrate (ES) complex rather than free enzyme, lowering both apparent Km and Vmax?
questions.explain: Uncompetitive inhibition occurs when an inhibitor binds only to the ES complex, forming an inactive ESI species and reducing both Vmax and apparent Km by the same factor. On a Lineweaver-Burk plot, this produces parallel lines.

open.q: Which reversible inhibitor binds only to the ES complex and lowers both apparent Km and Vmax?

questions.q: A patient presents with severe metabolic acidosis and visual disturbances after ingesting methanol. Ethanol is administered intravenously because it competes with methanol for which hepatic enzyme?
questions.explain: Alcohol dehydrogenase oxidizes methanol to formaldehyde and formic acid, which causes optic nerve toxicity and metabolic acidosis. Ethanol acts as a competitive substrate for alcohol dehydrogenase, slowing toxic metabolite formation until methanol is cleared.

open.q: Ethanol treats methanol poisoning by competing with methanol for which enzyme?

questions.q: A patient develops prolonged muscle paralysis after receiving succinylcholine during anesthesia because of a genetic variant of which plasma enzyme?
questions.explain: Plasma butyrylcholinesterase (pseudocholinesterase) normally hydrolyzes succinylcholine before most of it reaches the motor end-plate. Variants with markedly reduced activity prolong succinylcholine action and cause prolonged apnea.

open.q: Deficiency or variant form of which plasma enzyme prolongs neuromuscular blockade after succinylcholine?

questions.q: Which sigmoidal kinetic behavior is characteristic of many allosteric enzymes?
options: Cooperative binding of substrate across multiple subunits
Strict compliance with first-order kinetics at all substrate levels
Complete absence of regulatory effector sites
Irreversible covalent modification with every catalytic turn
questions.explain: Allosteric enzymes frequently possess multiple subunits and regulatory sites, showing cooperative substrate binding that produces a sigmoidal velocity-versus-[S] curve. Allosteric effectors shift the curve left (activators) or right (inhibitors).

open.q: What property of multimeric allosteric enzymes produces a sigmoidal substrate-saturation curve?

questions.q: Which covalent modification commonly regulates metabolic enzymes by adding a phosphoryl group from ATP to serine, threonine, or tyrosine residues?
questions.explain: Protein kinases transfer the gamma-phosphate of ATP onto hydroxyl groups of serine, threonine, or tyrosine residues, while protein phosphatases remove it. Phosphorylation can activate or inhibit target enzymes depending on the pathway.

open.q: Which covalent modification is catalyzed by protein kinases on serine, threonine, or tyrosine residues?

questions.q: What are isoenzymes (isozymes)?
options: Different protein forms of an enzyme that catalyze the same reaction
Enzymes that catalyze completely different chemical reactions
Cofactors bound to apoenzymes during electron transfer
Lipid-soluble hormones that induce gene transcription
questions.explain: Isoenzymes are distinct molecular forms of an enzyme (often encoded by different genes or differing in subunit composition, such as lactate dehydrogenase LDH1-LDH5) that catalyze the same reaction. They often differ in tissue distribution and kinetic properties.

open.q: How are isoenzymes defined in biochemistry?
accept: different forms of an enzyme catalyzing the same reaction
distinct enzyme variants with the same catalytic activity

questions.q: In a patient with acute myocardial infarction, which cardiac-specific biomarker rises in plasma within hours and remains elevated for several days?
questions.explain: Cardiac troponins I and T are highly specific and sensitive markers of myocardial cell injury, rising within 3 to 6 hours and remaining elevated for days. CK-MB (creatine kinase-MB) also rises early in myocardial injury but normalizes sooner.

open.q: Which cardiac biomarker is preferred for diagnosing acute myocardial injury due to its high cardiac specificity and prolonged elevation?

questions.q: What does a negative standard free energy change (delta G-nought < 0) indicate about a chemical reaction under standard conditions?
options: The forward reaction is exergonic under standard conditions
The reaction rate is infinitely fast
questions.explain: A negative standard free energy change (delta G-nought < 0) means products have lower standard free energy than reactants, corresponding to an equilibrium constant Keq > 1. Free energy change determines thermodynamic spontaneity, not reaction velocity.

open.q: What does a negative delta G-nought value indicate about a reaction under standard conditions?

questions.q: How is the actual free energy change (delta G) of a reaction related to the standard free energy change (delta G-nought) and reaction quotient (Q)?
options: delta G = delta G-nought + RT ln(Q)
delta G = delta G-nought - RT ln(Q)
delta G = delta G-nought * RT * Q
delta G = RT / (delta G-nought + ln Q)
questions.explain: The actual free energy change is given by delta G = delta G-nought + RT ln([products]/[reactants]), where R is the gas constant and T is absolute temperature. Even a reaction with positive delta G-nought can proceed in cells if product levels are kept very low.

open.q: Write the equation relating actual free energy change (delta G) to standard free energy change (delta G-nought) and reactant/product concentrations.
accept: delta G = delta G-nought + RT ln([products]/[reactants])

questions.q: Why does ATP hydrolysis to ADP and inorganic phosphate release a large amount of free energy under physiological conditions?
options: Relief of phosphate repulsion and resonance stabilisation of products
Formation of a covalent bond without water
Inorganic phosphate becomes a strong acid
All adenine carbon bonds are broken
questions.explain: At physiological pH, ATP carries multiple negatively charged phosphate oxygens that repel one another; hydrolysis relieves this electrostatic repulsion and yields products (ADP and Pi) with greater resonance stabilization and solvation. Thus ATP has a high phosphoryl group transfer potential.

open.q: What structural factors account for the large negative free energy of ATP hydrolysis?
accept: electrostatic repulsion relief and resonance stabilization
charge repulsion and resonance stabilization of products

questions.q: Which high-energy compound has a higher phosphoryl transfer potential than ATP and can donate a phosphate group to ADP to regenerate ATP in skeletal muscle?
questions.explain: Phosphocreatine has a more negative standard free energy of phosphate hydrolysis (about -43 kJ/mol) than ATP (about -30.5 kJ/mol), allowing creatine kinase to transfer phosphate to ADP during intense muscle contraction. Glucose-6-phosphate has a lower phosphoryl transfer potential than ATP.

open.q: Which high-energy phosphagen stores phosphoryl groups in muscle to rapidly regenerate ATP from ADP?

questions.q: What is substrate-level phosphorylation?
options: Direct transfer of phosphate from a high-energy intermediate to ADP
ATP synthesis driven by the mitochondrial proton gradient
Phosphate addition to sugar without ATP formation
questions.explain: Substrate-level phosphorylation synthesizes ATP or GTP directly by transferring a high-energy phosphate group from a substrate intermediate (such as 1,3-bisphosphoglycerate or phosphoenolpyruvate) to ADP. It does not require oxygen or an electron transport chain.

open.q: How is ATP synthesized during substrate-level phosphorylation?
accept: direct phosphoryl transfer from a phosphorylated substrate to ADP
transfer of phosphate from a high-energy metabolic intermediate to ADP

questions.q: In which cellular compartment is the mitochondrial electron transport chain (respiratory chain) located in eukaryotes?
questions.explain: The respiratory chain complexes (Complexes I-IV) and ATP synthase are embedded in the inner mitochondrial membrane, which is impermeable to ions and maintains the proton electrochemical gradient. The citric acid cycle occurs in the mitochondrial matrix (except succinate dehydrogenase on the inner membrane).

open.q: In which membrane of the mitochondrion are the electron transport chain complexes located?

questions.q: Which molecule serves as the final electron acceptor at Complex IV (cytochrome c oxidase) of the mitochondrial electron transport chain?
questions.explain: Complex IV (cytochrome c oxidase) transfers electrons from reduced cytochrome c to molecular oxygen, reducing O2 to water (H2O). Without oxygen as the terminal electron acceptor, electron flow backs up and oxidative phosphorylation stops.

open.q: Which molecule accepts electrons at the end of the mitochondrial electron transport chain to form water?

questions.q: Which mobile lipid carrier shuttles electrons from Complexes I and II to Complex III within the inner mitochondrial membrane?
questions.explain: Coenzyme Q (ubiquinone) is a lipid-soluble benzoquinone carrier that diffuses within the inner mitochondrial membrane core, accepting electrons from NADH dehydrogenase (Complex I) and succinate dehydrogenase (Complex II) and passing them to Complex III. Cytochrome c is a peripheral heme protein on the outer face of the inner membrane.

open.q: Which lipid-soluble electron carrier transfers electrons from Complexes I and II to Complex III?

questions.q: According to Mitchell's chemiosmotic hypothesis, what directly drives ATP synthesis by ATP synthase (Complex V)?
options: Protons move down their electrochemical gradient across the inner mitochondrial membrane
Glucose is oxidised in the intermembrane space
GTP is hydrolysed in the cytosol
questions.explain: Electron transport pumps protons from the matrix into the intermembrane space, creating a proton-motive force (pH and electrical gradient). Re-entry of protons through ATP synthase drives rotary catalysis to phosphorylate ADP into ATP.

open.q: What gradient across the inner mitochondrial membrane drives ATP synthesis via ATP synthase?

questions.q: What happens to electron transport and oxygen consumption when a chemical uncoupler (such as 2,4-dinitrophenol) dissipates the proton gradient across the inner mitochondrial membrane?
options: Electron transport and O2 use continue, but ATP synthesis falls and heat is released
Electron transport and O2 consumption stop
ATP synthesis rises while oxygen use stops
Complex I no longer oxidises NADH
questions.explain: Uncouplers carry protons back across the inner membrane independently of ATP synthase, collapsing the proton gradient so ATP synthesis falls while electron transport and O2 consumption proceed rapidly and release free energy as heat. Physiological uncoupling via UCP1 (thermogenin) generates heat in brown adipose tissue.

open.q: How does an uncoupler of oxidative phosphorylation affect oxygen consumption and ATP synthesis?
accept: maintains or increases oxygen consumption while reducing ATP synthesis
uncouples respiration from ATP synthesis and increases heat

questions.q: A patient exposed to cyanide presents with sudden collapse, lactic acidosis, bright venous blood, and severe cellular hypoxia because cyanide binds tightly to which component of the respiratory chain?
questions.explain: Cyanide binds tightly to the ferric/heme iron of cytochrome c oxidase (Complex IV), halting terminal electron transfer to oxygen and blocking both electron transport and oxidative phosphorylation. Cells rely on anaerobic glycolysis, producing excess lactate and lactic acidosis.

open.q: Which respiratory chain complex is inhibited by cyanide poisoning?

questions.q: A competitive inhibitor is added to an enzyme-catalysed reaction. Which kinetic change is expected when substrate concentration is increased sufficiently?
options: Apparent Km increases while Vmax remains unchanged
Vmax decreases while Km remains unchanged
questions.explain: A competitive inhibitor competes with substrate at the active site. It increases the apparent Km because more substrate is needed to reach half-maximal velocity, but sufficiently high substrate can overcome inhibition, leaving Vmax unchanged.

open.q: How does a reversible competitive inhibitor affect apparent Km and Vmax?
accept: Km increases and Vmax is unchanged

questions.q: A non-competitive inhibitor binds at a site distinct from the active site and reduces catalytic activity. In the ideal pure non-competitive model, what happens?
options: Vmax decreases while Km remains unchanged
Km increases while Vmax remains unchanged
Both Km and Vmax remain unchanged
questions.explain: In pure non-competitive inhibition, inhibitor binding reduces the amount of catalytically active enzyme without changing substrate binding affinity. Vmax decreases while Km remains unchanged.

open.q: What happens to Vmax and Km in pure non-competitive enzyme inhibition?

questions.q: An enzyme is produced as an inactive precursor and becomes active after a specific peptide segment is cleaved. What is this type of regulation called?
questions.explain: Zymogens are inactive enzyme precursors activated by specific proteolytic cleavage. This mechanism is important for digestive enzymes and proteases of the coagulation cascade, allowing activation to be spatially and temporally controlled.

open.q: What is a zymogen, and how is it commonly activated?
accept: An inactive enzyme precursor activated by specific proteolytic cleavage

questions.q: An enzyme transfers a phosphate group from ATP to glucose to form glucose-6-phosphate. To which major enzyme class does it belong?
questions.explain: Hexokinase transfers a phosphoryl group from ATP to glucose. Enzymes that transfer functional groups from one molecule to another are transferases (EC class 2).

open.q: Which major enzyme class includes kinases that transfer phosphate groups?

questions.q: A patient with poor dietary intake has impaired aminotransferase activity. Which vitamin-derived coenzyme is required by these enzymes?
questions.explain: Aminotransferases require pyridoxal phosphate (PLP), the active coenzyme form of vitamin B6. PLP forms a transient Schiff-base intermediate and facilitates transfer of amino groups.

open.q: Which vitamin-derived coenzyme is required for aminotransferase reactions?

questions.q: A patient with myocardial injury has a raised serum enzyme marker. Which statement best describes an isoenzyme?
options: Different molecular forms of an enzyme that catalyse the same reaction
An inactive precursor of an enzyme
A coenzyme permanently bound to an enzyme
A substrate that inhibits enzyme activity
questions.explain: Isoenzymes are distinct molecular forms of an enzyme that catalyse the same reaction but differ in structure, physicochemical properties or tissue distribution. Their patterns can help identify the tissue source of enzyme release.

open.q: Define isoenzymes.
accept: Different molecular forms of an enzyme catalysing the same reaction
Multiple forms of an enzyme with the same catalytic activity

questions.q: The end product of a metabolic pathway binds to an enzyme near the beginning of the pathway and reduces its activity. What is this mechanism?
questions.explain: Feedback inhibition occurs when a downstream product inhibits an earlier enzyme, often the first committed step, limiting unnecessary product formation and conserving cellular resources.

open.q: What is feedback inhibition in a metabolic pathway?
accept: The pathway end product inhibits an earlier enzyme in the pathway
End-product inhibition of an upstream enzyme

questions.q: An enzyme follows Michaelis-Menten kinetics. At a substrate concentration equal to Km, what fraction of Vmax is the reaction velocity?
questions.explain: For a Michaelis-Menten enzyme, v = Vmax[S]/(Km+[S]). When [S] equals Km, velocity is Vmax/2.

open.q: What is the reaction velocity when substrate concentration equals Km?

questions.q: An enzyme-catalysed reaction is measured at saturating substrate concentration. If the amount of active enzyme is doubled, what is expected, assuming other conditions remain constant?
options: Vmax doubles while Km remains unchanged
Km doubles while Vmax remains unchanged
Both Km and Vmax are halved
questions.explain: At saturating substrate concentration, reaction velocity is proportional to the amount of active enzyme. Doubling enzyme concentration therefore doubles Vmax. Km is an intrinsic kinetic parameter for the enzyme-substrate interaction under the stated conditions and is not changed simply by increasing enzyme concentration.

open.q: What happens to Vmax and Km when active enzyme concentration is doubled at saturating substrate concentration?
accept: Maximum velocity doubles while Km stays the same

questions.q: An uncoupling agent increases proton permeability of the inner mitochondrial membrane. Which outcome is expected?
options: Increased oxygen consumption with reduced ATP synthesis efficiency
Reduced electron transport and increased ATP yield
Complete inhibition of substrate oxidation with increased proton gradient
Increased ATP synthesis because the proton gradient becomes steeper
questions.explain: Uncouplers dissipate the proton-motive force. Electron transport and oxygen consumption may continue or increase, but less energy is conserved as ATP and more is released as heat.

open.q: What happens to oxidative phosphorylation when an uncoupler dissipates the proton gradient?
accept: Oxygen consumption continues or increases while ATP synthesis falls and heat production rises
